claims.text: The initial material is an as-cast eutectic NbMoCrTiAl-based high-entropy alloy.
A ball-milled and spark-plasma-sintered NbMoCrTiAl composite contains in-situ reinforcement particles.
The reinforced NbMoCrTiAl composite has high compressive strength.
The reinforced NbMoCrTiAl composite exhibits cleavage fracture and essentially no room-temperature ductility.
Adding 1–2 at.% V will promote formation of V-rich precipitates.
The V-rich precipitates will be nanoscale and coherent.
The V-rich precipitates will form both at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
The V-rich precipitates will refine the microstructure.
The V-rich precipitates will improve interphase bonding.
Coherent V-rich precipitates will obstruct dislocation motion.
Precipitation and grain-boundary strengthening caused by the V addition will increase strength.
Ductile, well-bonded precipitate interfaces will reduce stress concentration and crack propagation.
Reduced stress concentration and crack propagation will increase elongation to failure.
Adding 1–2 at.% V is expected to increase yield or ultimate strength by approximately 20–30% relative to the V-free alloy.
Adding 1–2 at.% V is expected to produce a significant increase in elongation to failure relative to the V-free alloy.
The cited V-free NbMoCrTiAl material made by ball milling and spark plasma sintering has high strength but very low ductility because it fails by cleavage.
The strength-and-ductility improvement requires retention of a controlled eutectic phase constitution.
Processing that prevents coherent precipitate formation may eliminate the proposed improvement.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis calls for thermal histories and cooling rates similar to the baseline, but the cited baseline uses prolonged ball milling followed by SPS at 1700 °C, whereas the proposed experiment uses melt casting and controlled cooling. These are materially different processing routes.

The material is alternately described as as-cast, as a ball-milled/SPS particle-reinforced composite, and as a melt-cast eutectic alloy. Consequently, the identity of the baseline against which the V addition is to be compared is inconsistent.
